definition: ASR-complete is, by analogy to "NP-completeness" in complexity theory, a term to indicate that the difficulty of a computational problem is equivalent to solving the central automatic speech recognition problem, i.e.
details: recognize and understanding spoken language. Unlike "NP-completeness", this term is typically used informally. Such problems are hypothesised to include: Spoken natural language understanding Understanding speech from far-field microphones, i.e. handling the reverbation and background noise These problems are easy for humans to do (in fact, they are described directly in terms of imitating humans). Some systems can solve very simple restricted versions of these problems, but none can solve them in their full generality.

explainer.lead: ASR-complete is an informal label for a problem whose difficulty is equivalent to fully recognizing and understanding spoken language. It signals that a tidy solution to a narrow speech task is still far from handling speech in its full generality.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a puzzle that is just as hard as perfectly hearing and understanding everything people say, even in a noisy room. Calling it ASR-complete is like saying, “Solve this, and you have solved the big listening-and-understanding puzzle too.” People can do this easily, but machines can so far handle only simpler, limited versions.
tiers.practitioner: The label may be applied informally to spoken natural-language understanding or to handling far-field microphone speech with reverberation and background noise. It is a warning about generality: success on a restricted version should not be presented as solving the complete problem. It is not a rigorous complexity classification or a claim supported by a formal reduction.
tiers.paperLevel: By analogy with NP-completeness, a problem P is described as ASR-complete when solving P is equivalent in difficulty to solving the central automatic speech recognition problem: recognizing and understanding spoken language. The usage is informal and hypothesis-driven rather than a formally established complexity class. Proposed examples include spoken natural-language understanding and general far-field speech understanding; existing systems address restricted cases but not these problems in full generality.

explainer.example: Consider understanding speech from a far-field microphone in a room with reverberation and background noise. A system might manage a simple, restricted version, but handling the task in full generality is hypothesized to be as difficult as recognizing and understanding spoken language overall.

usedIn.name: Spoken natural-language understanding
usedIn.detail: Understanding the meaning of spoken language is hypothesized to be ASR-complete.

usedIn.name: Far-field speech recognition
usedIn.detail: Understanding speech captured by distant microphones requires coping with reverberation and background noise.

explainer.intuition: Some speech problems seem to contain the whole challenge of human-like listening and understanding. ASR-complete borrows the language of NP-completeness to express that idea, but only as an informal analogy.
howItWorks: Start with a problem involving the recognition or understanding of speech.
Ask whether solving it in full generality would be equivalent to solving the central speech-recognition-and-understanding problem.
If so, the problem may be described informally as ASR-complete.
Distinguish this general problem from restricted versions that current systems can already solve.
explainer.whyItMatters: The term separates genuinely general speech understanding from success on narrow, constrained tasks. It also emphasizes the gap between problems people find easy and problems machines cannot yet solve in full generality.
misconceptions: ASR-complete is not a formally defined complexity class like NP-complete.
The label does not mean every automatic speech recognition task is unsolved.
Solving a restricted version does not establish a solution to the general problem.
